passage: Ujjwal, you want to drag your friend out of that group? Let your Farhan-chacha tell you what I did wrong. In 1995 my friend Suresh joined a 'brotherhood' in Aligarh that made him wear white and stop eating with us. I was furious and scared for him. So I made a plan with two others: we'd tell him his mother was ill, bring him home, and not let him go back. It worked for one night. The next morning he found out, walked back, and told the group, 'You were right, my friends are against me.' He didn't speak to me for two years. The second time, I did it differently. I wrote him a letter every month, just news from the mohalla. When he came to a wedding, I sat with him and asked what he found there. Once, only once, I shared an article about the group's leader. Five years later he came home by himself. So, Ujjwal: no tricks. Keep the door open.

qa.q: What did the group make Suresh wear?
qa.a: The group made Suresh wear white.

qa.q: How did young Farhan feel when Suresh joined the brotherhood?
qa.a: Farhan felt furious and scared for Suresh.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Farhan's approach?
qa.a: Seeing the trick backfire and prove the group right, after which he wrote monthly letters, asked open questions and shared information only once.

qa.q: How did Suresh see the plot to keep him home?
qa.a: Suresh saw it as proof that his friends were against him, just as the group had said.

grounding: An uncle recalls how a secret plot to rescue a friend from a worrying group backfired, and how steady contact and open questions kept the door open.

passage: Exams started in three days, but Vikas couldn't study. His roommate Anand had moved his things out to live with the 'Dawn Collective', and tonight's heavy rain had wrecked Vikas's plan to visit. He opened a message to Anand and typed: 'That group is a cult and you're an idiot for falling for it.' He looked at it for a long minute. It was what he felt. It was also exactly what the group would want Anand to read. He deleted it. Instead he wrote: 'Hey. The room's weird without your terrible music. How are you finding it there? What do you do all day?' Anand replied after an hour, long and happy: meditation, farm work, 'real brothers'. Vikas didn't argue. He asked, 'Do they let you keep your phone and your own money?' A pause. 'Mostly.' Vikas noted that 'mostly'. 'After exams, can I come see the farm?' 'Yes!' Vikas finally opened his textbook.

qa.q: When did exams start?
qa.a: Exams started in three days.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling as he typed the first message?
qa.a: Vikas felt angry and frightened for Anand, wanting to call the group a cult.

qa.q: Why was deleting the first message wise?
qa.a: Mocking would push Anand closer to the group; open questions kept contact and revealed the 'mostly' about phone and money.

qa.q: How does Anand describe life in the group?
qa.a: Anand sounds happy, talking about meditation, farm work and 'real brothers'.

grounding: Shows a worried friend resisting the urge to mock and instead keeping contact through warm, open questions during a hectic exam week.

passage: Note from Parveen, political science lecturer, after Tuesday's tutorial. Dhruv, usually calm, arrived shaking. He said that if 'the other side' won the state election, everything he valued, his friends' freedom to speak, his sister's job, would be destroyed. He had been watching videos until 3 a.m. He wasn't performing; the fear was real. I didn't argue with his values. I asked where the claims in the videos came from. He didn't know. We picked three claims and checked them together against the election commission's data and two newspapers with different leanings. One was true, one was exaggerated, one was invented. He went quiet, then said, 'Someone's selling me panic.' We talked about what he could actually do: vote, volunteer with the voter-registration drive in his ward, talk to neighbours. He also admitted he had started calling a classmate 'the enemy'. He said he'd stop. I'll check in after the results.

qa.q: Until what time had Dhruv been watching videos?
qa.a: Dhruv had been watching videos until 3 a.m.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he arrived?
qa.a: Dhruv felt sincerely afraid, shaking at the thought that the other side's win would destroy what he valued.

qa.q: Why did checking the claims help Dhruv?
qa.a: Checking three claims against official data and differently leaning papers showed that some of the fear was being sold to him.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's classmate have felt being called 'the enemy'?
qa.a: The classmate may have felt hurt and pushed away just for holding different views.

grounding: A lecturer's note shows sincere fear of the other side winning, checked against varied sources, and turned toward voting and local work instead of treating opponents as enemies.

passage: Thursday night. Saurabh here, and I can't sleep again. Every reel tonight said that if the other party wins, my town's college will close, farmers will be ruined, and people like me will be 'finished'. My chest has been tight all day. At lunch I nearly stopped talking to Mohit because he supports them. He said, 'Do you really think I want your college closed?' and I didn't have an answer. So tonight I did something different. I turned off reels, opened the official budget documents and two newspapers I don't usually read, and checked the college claim. It was a rumour from a page with no name. Some of my worries are still real. But some were sold to me like fear in a packet. Tomorrow I'm signing up for the voter-help desk at the panchayat office. And I'm buying Mohit a samosa.

qa.q: Where is Saurabh signing up to help tomorrow?
qa.a: Saurabh is signing up for the voter-help desk at the panchayat office.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling all day?
qa.a: Saurabh felt anxious and afraid, chest tight from the reels' warnings.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do tonight that was wise?
qa.a: Turned off reels, checked the college claim in official documents and varied newspapers, and chose local action.

qa.q: What does Mohit's question suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests Mohit feels hurt at being treated as an enemy and wants Saurabh to see a friend who disagrees.

grounding: A diary shows sincere political fear fed by reels, then checked against varied sources and turned into local action without treating a friend as an enemy.

passage:
Dear Dhruv-mama,
I'm writing because I didn't want to say this at the table on Sunday, with Nani's birthday cake still out.
When you said my views were 'brainwashed' by my college, I felt insulted, and my face went hot. You know I had an answer ready; I think you wanted it. But I didn't want Nani's eightieth to end in shouting, so I said, 'Mama, I don't want to argue tonight,' and asked about your new scooter instead. I know that annoyed you.
I'm happy to talk about politics with you, honestly. Not when we're both heated, and not with 'brainwashed' in it. I read, I think, I sometimes change my mind. So, I hope, do you.
Next month, when I'm home, could we go for a walk and talk properly? You can tell me what worries you, and I'll tell you what worries me.
With respect,
Abhinav

qa.q: Whose birthday was it on Sunday?
qa.a: It was Nani's eightieth birthday.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel when called 'brainwashed'?
qa.a: Abhinav felt insulted, face hot, with a sharp answer ready.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do at dinner that was wise?
qa.a: Abhinav calmly declined to argue and changed the subject to protect Nani's birthday, then offered a calmer talk later.

qa.q: How might Dhruv-mama feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Dhruv-mama may feel a little embarrassed but respected, invited to a proper talk instead of a fight.

grounding: A letter shows a relative calling Abhinav's views brainwashed at a family dinner, and Abhinav declining to debate while heated and offering a calmer talk.

passage: Last Diwali I ruined dinner. I'm Gargi, and I'll own it. My uncle Varun said my views were 'brainwashed' by my Delhi college, and I shot back that his were copied from forwarded messages. He raised his voice, I raised mine, Dadi started crying, and my mother didn't speak to me all the way home. This Diwali he started again, over the kheer. 'Still brainwashed, Gargi?' Everyone froze. I could feel the whole speech ready in my throat. Instead I breathed and said, calmly, 'Chacha, I'd love to talk politics with you some day, but not at Diwali dinner. How's the new shop?' He blinked. Then he started talking about the shop. It wasn't magic. He muttered something later. But Dadi smiled at me across the table, and nobody cried. I still think I'm right. I just don't need to win over the kheer.

qa.q: What happened at last Diwali's dinner?
qa.a: Gargi shot back at the uncle, both raised their voices, Dadi cried, and Gargi's mother stayed silent all the way home.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when her uncle said 'Still brainwashed'?
qa.a: Gargi felt insulted and angry, with the whole speech ready.

qa.q: What changed between last Diwali and this one?
qa.a: Last year Gargi escalated and dinner was ruined; this year Gargi declined calmly and changed the subject.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt this year compared with last?
qa.a: Dadi was likely relieved and happy, smiling instead of crying.

grounding: A spoken account contrasts escalating with a relative who calls one's views brainwashed and, a year later, calmly declining the debate and changing the subject.

passage: Every Sunday in the Lucknow flat, Dadaji read the newspaper aloud and commented on every politician, and every Sunday Hrithik smiled politely and thought, He's so out of date. Once Hrithik rolled his eyes behind the paper, and his mother, Nirmala, caught it and frowned. This Sunday, when Dadaji said that only strong rulers kept a country safe, Hrithik put down his phone. 'Dadaji, what made you feel that way?' The old man looked surprised. Then he talked, for forty minutes: about the riots he saw as a boy from his family's rooftop, about neighbours who disappeared, about how safe order felt afterwards. Hrithik had never heard any of it. When Dadaji finished, Hrithik said, 'I see it differently, because I've grown up with other fears. But I understand yours now.' Dadaji grunted and handed him the sports page. 'Read me the cricket.'

qa.q: What did Dadaji read aloud every Sunday?
qa.a: Dadaji read the newspaper aloud.

qa.q: What did Hrithik feel toward Dadaji's views before this Sunday?
qa.a: Hrithik felt quiet contempt, thinking Dadaji was out of date, even rolling his eyes.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking what made Dadaji feel that way, then sharing his own view without trying to win, which let him understand and value his grandfather.

qa.q: How might Dadaji have felt being asked about his experiences?
qa.a: Dadaji was surprised and seemed glad to be heard, talking for forty minutes and then sharing the sports page.

grounding: Shows a grandson's hidden contempt for his grandfather's politics giving way to asking what shaped those views and valuing the person over the position.

passage:
'These young people with their phones know nothing about the country,' Ajoba said, jabbing a finger at the TV.
Nilesh felt the old irritation. He'd heard it all before. 'Ajoba, can I ask you something without us fighting?'
'Ask.'
'Why do you trust that party so much? Really. What happened that made you trust them?'
Ajoba muted the TV. 'In 1972, the drought. Our village had nothing. A young man from their side came with trucks of grain when nobody else came. I was nineteen. I carried sacks with him for a month.'
Nilesh was quiet. 'I didn't know that.'
'You never asked.'
'I'm asking now. I see them differently, Ajoba, because of things I've seen at college. But I get why you trust them.'
'And I don't have to agree with you.'
'No. You don't.'
From the kitchen, Aaji called, 'Jagdish, are you two fighting?'
'No,' Ajoba called back, almost smiling. 'We're talking.'

qa.q: What happened in 1972?
qa.a: There was a drought, and a young man from that party came with trucks of grain.

qa.q: What did Nilesh feel when Ajoba said young people knew nothing?
qa.a: Nilesh felt the old irritation rising.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that put the person above the position?
qa.a: He asked what experience shaped Ajoba's trust, listened, and shared his own view without trying to win.

qa.q: How does Ajoba describe the conversation at the end?
qa.a: Ajoba calls it talking, not fighting, almost smiling.

grounding: Shows a grandson who disagrees with his grandfather's politics asking what experiences shaped them and sharing his own view without trying to win.

passage: After the municipal election in their small town in Burdwan district, Chetan went through his phone like a broom: he unfriended, blocked or left every group where someone had backed the other side. Forty-two people, including his school friend Bidisha, who had once argued with him for an hour at the tea stall and then bought him a second cup. For a week it felt wonderful. His feed agreed with him on everything. Then he noticed he had started believing things without checking, because nobody pushed back. And the tea-stall evenings felt emptier. One night he saw a post Bidisha had shared about repairing the town library, something they both cared about. He couldn't comment; he had blocked her. He sat on the steps outside his house feeling oddly alone. The man who had abused him in the comments, he kept blocked. Bidisha he unblocked, and messaged: 'Library project? I'd help. We can still disagree about the rest.'

qa.q: How many people did Chetan unfriend, block or leave?
qa.a: Chetan cut off forty-two people.

qa.q: What did Chetan feel after a week of an agreeing feed?
qa.a: Chetan felt relieved at first, then oddly alone and uneasy about believing things without checking.

qa.q: What balance did Chetan find?
qa.a: He kept blocking the man who abused him but unblocked Bidisha, keeping respectful disagreement in his life.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel getting Chetan's message?
qa.a: Bidisha may feel pleased and relieved to have her friend back, even if they still disagree.

grounding: Shows relief after cutting off everyone who disagrees turning into isolation, and Chetan keeping boundaries against abuse while letting respectful dissent back in.

passage: During the heated months before the national vote, Mei muted and unfollowed everyone in Melbourne who didn't share her views, including her old debate partner, Layla. The relief was instant: no more arguments at midnight, no more tightness in her chest. Her feed felt like a warm room full of people nodding. Three weeks later, in a university seminar, the lecturer asked the class to explain the strongest case for the other side. Mei opened her mouth and realised she couldn't. She had only ever heard it mocked. On the tram home, she felt a strange loneliness, surrounded by agreement. That night she scrolled back to Layla's profile. Layla had never been cruel, only different. Mei kept blocked the two accounts that had sent her abusive messages. She re-followed Layla and sent her a note: 'I miss arguing with you. Coffee? I need to hear the other side from someone who won't sneer.' Layla replied with a coffee cup.

qa.q: What did the lecturer ask the class to explain?
qa.a: The lecturer asked them to explain the strongest case for the other side.

qa.q: What did Mei feel on the tram home?
qa.a: Mei felt a strange loneliness, surrounded by agreement.

qa.q: What boundary did Mei keep, and what did she change?
qa.a: She kept the two abusive accounts blocked but re-followed Layla, keeping respectful dissent in her life.

qa.q: How does Layla respond to Mei's message?
qa.a: Layla replies warmly with a coffee cup, open to meeting again.

grounding: Shows the relief and later isolation of an echo chamber, and Mei keeping boundaries against abuse while welcoming back respectful disagreement.

passage: In the hostel TV room in Aligarh, Rafiq cheered when the young minister finished his speech. Rafiq had followed him for two years: his clean-water scheme in Rafiq's home district, his calm voice, the way he took questions. Rafiq felt proud just watching him. Then Irfan, from the next room, said, 'The water scheme's only reached half the villages he promised, you know.' Rafiq felt heat rise in his neck, as if Irfan had insulted his own family. 'You just hate anyone doing good.' Irfan held up his hands. 'I like him too. I'm just saying the numbers.' Rafiq stomped back to his room. An hour later, still irritated, he opened the district data site to prove Irfan wrong. Irfan was right: about half. Rafiq sat with that. He still admired the minister. But he knocked on Irfan's door. 'You were right about the villages. I still think he's the best we've got. But he should fix that.'

qa.q: What scheme did the minister run in Rafiq's home district?
qa.a: The minister ran a clean-water scheme.

qa.q: What did Rafiq feel when Irfan mentioned the numbers?
qa.a: Rafiq felt angry and personally insulted, heat rising in his neck.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that kept his admiration honest?
qa.a: He checked the district data, admitted Irfan was right, and kept admiring the minister while saying the gap should be fixed.

qa.q: How does Irfan see the minister?
qa.a: Irfan likes him too but wants the numbers faced honestly.

grounding: Shows admiration for a political leader making criticism feel like a personal attack, until Rafiq checks the evidence and can criticise his own side.

passage:
Dear Rafiq,
I owe you an apology for the canteen on Friday.
When you said the chief minister's housing promise was mostly photo opportunities, I took it as if you'd insulted my own family. I called you jealous and walked off. You didn't deserve that.
I've admired her since school; she came to our village when I was twelve and shook my hand. I still admire her. But on Saturday I read the housing department's own figures, and you were closer to right than I wanted. Fewer than a third of the houses are finished.
I think I've been treating any criticism of her like criticism of me. That isn't loyalty, it's just touchiness. I want to be someone who can support a leader and still say, 'This part isn't good enough.'
Can we meet at the canteen this Friday? This time I'll listen properly.
Abhinav

qa.q: What did Rafiq say about the housing promise?
qa.a: Rafiq said it was mostly photo opportunities.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel when Rafiq criticised the chief minister?
qa.a: Abhinav felt insulted, as if Abhinav's own family had been attacked.

qa.q: What did Abhinav learn about admiring a leader?
qa.a: That Abhinav can keep supporting her while admitting the housing figures aren't good enough, instead of treating criticism as a personal attack.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rafiq may feel relieved and respected, invited back to talk after being called jealous.

grounding: A letter shows admiration for a leader turning criticism into a personal insult, and Abhinav checking the evidence and learning to criticise his own side.

passage: On the bus home in Buenos Aires, Lucia's feed served her a thirty-second clip: a politician she disliked, apparently laughing while a reporter described flooded homes. Fury shot through her. The comments were already a bonfire. Her thumb was on the share button, her own caption half typed: 'This is who they are.' Then she remembered her friend Camila, a journalism student, saying, 'If a clip makes you want to scream in under a minute, someone probably cut it that way.' Lucia took a breath. She searched for the full press conference. In the original, the politician had laughed at a colleague's joke twenty minutes earlier, and the clip had stitched it next to the flood question. Lucia felt a strange mix of relief and embarrassment. She deleted her caption. Then she sent the full video link to the two friends who had already shared the clip, with a short note: 'Checked the full thing. It's edited.'

qa.q: How long was the clip?
qa.a: The clip was thirty seconds long.

qa.q: What did Lucia feel when the clip first played?
qa.a: Lucia felt a jolt of fury, angry enough to share it at once.

qa.q: What did Lucia do instead of sharing?
qa.a: She paused, found the full press conference, deleted her caption, and sent the full link to friends who had shared the clip.

qa.q: What had Camila noticed about clips like this?
qa.a: Camila had learned that clips which make you want to scream fast are often cut that way on purpose.

grounding: Shows an edited viral clip provoking instant fury, and Lucia pausing, finding the full context and refusing to spread the outrage.

passage: In the media lab of the college library in Bhopal, Kashish's phone buzzed with a clip in the class group: students from another college apparently throwing stones at police, captioned 'This is what their side does.' Her jaw locked with fury; she had been arguing with that side all week. She was about to forward it to three more groups. At the next computer, Preeti, who helped run the college's fact-check club, glanced over. 'Where's it from?' Kashish didn't know. Preeti ran the clip through a reverse video search. It came from a different state, three years ago, in an unrelated clash. Only the caption was new. Kashish's anger turned into something colder, a feeling of being used. 'Someone wanted me angry,' she said. 'And I nearly helped.' She didn't forward it. Instead she posted in the class group: 'This clip is from three years ago, different state. Please check before sharing.' Two people deleted it.

qa.q: Where was the clip actually from?
qa.a: The clip was from a different state, three years ago, in an unrelated clash.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel once the search showed the truth?
qa.a: Kashish's fury turned into a colder feeling of being used, uneasy and a little ashamed at nearly helping.

qa.q: What did Kashish do instead of forwarding the clip?
qa.a: She posted a correction in the class group asking people to check before sharing.

qa.q: How does Preeti approach the clip?
qa.a: Preeti calmly asks where it's from and checks it, rather than reacting to it.

grounding: Shows a mislabelled clip meant to enrage, and a student pausing, checking its source and correcting it instead of spreading outrage.

passage:
'You slept here again?' Vishal nudged the bundle of posters on the floor of the campus climate club's office.
Vikas sat up, blinking. 'Clean-up planning ran late. We're doing the river bank on Sunday. Four hundred people signed up, Vishal. Four hundred!'
'That's amazing. You also missed two lab sessions this week.'
'The river can't wait.'
'Your degree can't either. And when did you last call home?'
Vikas rubbed his eyes. 'Last week? Maybe.'
'And you called Aman a "planet killer" for not joining.'
'He drives everywhere.'
'He also lent you his notes.' Vishal sat down on the posters. 'I love that you care this much. I just want you still caring in five years, not burnt out by December.'
Vikas was quiet. 'The club is the first thing that's made me feel useful here.'
'Keep it. Just sleep in your bed. Go to labs. And apologise to Aman.'
Vikas laughed weakly. 'Fine. After Sunday.'
'Before Sunday.'

qa.q: How many people signed up for the river bank drive?
qa.a: Four hundred people signed up.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel about the club?
qa.a: Vikas feels hopeful and useful; the club is the first thing that has given him direction there.

qa.q: What does Vishal want Vikas to protect, and why?
qa.a: Sleep, labs, calls home and friendships like Aman's, so the commitment lasts instead of burning out.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt being called a 'planet killer'?
qa.a: Aman may have felt hurt and judged, especially after lending Vikas his notes.

grounding: Shows a student whose cause gives his life direction, and a friend urging him to protect sleep, studies and relationships and not see non-members as enemies.

passage: I'm Neelam, and in my second year I gave everything to the evening literacy classes for domestic workers in our basti. I taught five nights a week, made the charts, chased funding, answered every call. For the first time in my life I knew why I got up in the morning. Then in March I fainted in the middle of a class. I hadn't eaten properly in days, and I'd failed two internal exams. Worse, I'd started snapping at friends who didn't volunteer, as if they were the problem. Shankar, the retired headmaster who started the classes, came to see me. He said, 'I've watched people give like this for one year and never come back. I need you for twenty.' So now I teach three nights, not five. I sleep. I passed my re-exams. I brought two friends along one evening, and neither of them is a bad person for coming only once. The cause is still my direction. It just doesn't eat me anymore.

qa.q: How many nights a week does Neelam teach now?
qa.a: Neelam teaches three nights a week now.

qa.q: What did the literacy classes make Neelam feel?
qa.a: Neelam felt a sense of purpose and hope, knowing why to get up each morning.

qa.q: What changes helped Neelam's commitment last?
qa.a: Teaching three nights instead of five, sleeping, passing re-exams, and not judging friends who help less.

qa.q: Why does Shankar want Neelam to slow down?
qa.a: Shankar has seen people give everything for a year and then leave, and wants Neelam around for twenty.

grounding: A first-person account of a cause giving life direction, near burnout and judging non-volunteers, and learning to protect health, studies and friendships so the commitment lasts.

passage: The night before the student march in Paris, Ines couldn't sleep. She kept imagining police lines, batons, her face on the news, and her parents in Porto seeing it. Her flatmate Bao, who had marched before, sat with her in the kitchen. 'Fear's okay. It keeps you sensible. Let's plan.' They wrote a contact number on each other's arms in marker, packed ID cards, water and a phone charger. Bao showed her the organisers' page on rights at protests and the legal-aid number posted there. 'We stay together. We stick to the route. If it turns ugly, we leave by a side street, no hero stuff.' In the morning the march was loud and joyful: drums, painted banners, grandmothers with placards. Near the end, a small group started pushing at a barrier. Ines's heart jumped. Bao touched her arm. They left by the side street, as planned, and called Ines's mother from a café, laughing a little with relief.

qa.q: What did Ines and Bao write on each other's arms?
qa.a: They wrote a contact number on each other's arms in marker.

qa.q: What was Ines afraid of the night before?
qa.a: Ines was afraid of police lines, batons, being on the news, and her parents seeing it.

qa.q: What made their plan safe?
qa.a: Staying together, carrying ID, water and a contact number, knowing the rights page and legal-aid number, and leaving by a side street when it turned tense.

qa.q: How does Bao see Ines's fear?
qa.a: Bao sees the fear as normal and sensible, something to plan around.

grounding: Shows fear before a march met with preparation: knowing one's rights, going with others, carrying ID and a contact, following the peaceful plan and leaving when it turned unsafe.

passage: In the student union office of the Kolkata university, the night before the march over hostel fees, Ishita ran the briefing with a whiteboard. Darshan sat at the back, knee bouncing. He had never marched before. He kept thinking of lathi charges he had seen on the news, and of his father, a government clerk, who had said, 'Don't get your name in any list.' Ishita went through it calmly: the permitted route, the marshals in orange bibs, the legal-aid volunteer's number to write on your wrist, ID in your pocket, water, a buddy for everyone. 'If anything turns violent, from any side, we disperse. Nobody is a hero.' Darshan raised his hand. 'What if someone pushes us to break the line?' 'Then you walk away and find a marshal.' He felt his knee slow down. He texted his father: 'Going with the group. Peaceful route, marshals, I'll call you at 1 p.m.' His father replied: 'Call at 1. Not 1:05.'

qa.q: What colour bibs do the marshals wear?
qa.a: The marshals wear orange bibs.

qa.q: What does Darshan's bouncing knee suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Darshan feels nervous and afraid of violence and of his father's reaction.

qa.q: Which parts of Ishita's plan keep marchers safe?
qa.a: The permitted route, marshals, a legal-aid number on the wrist, ID, water, a buddy, and dispersing if anything turns violent.

qa.q: What does Darshan's father's reply suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggests he is worried but accepting, wanting an exact check-in for reassurance.

grounding: Shows a first-time marcher's fear of police and family reaction eased by a peaceful plan, rights information, a buddy, ID, a contact and a rule to leave if it turns unsafe.

passage: I'm Ganga, and our river-protection group was the closest thing to family I had in college. We'd sat in the rain together, shared tiffins at dawn. So when Zeenat, our coordinator, suggested posting the home address of the factory manager who'd been dumping waste, 'so people can go and tell him what they think', everyone cheered. I felt sick. His kids lived there. But I said nothing that night; I didn't want to be the one who spoiled things. At home I couldn't sleep. The next morning, before anything was posted, I called Zeenat. 'I love this group. That's why I'm saying it: posting his address could get someone hurt, and it would make us the story instead of the river.' She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, 'Say it at the meeting. I think others feel it too.' I did. Three people nodded at once. We filed a complaint with the pollution board instead, and held a sit-in at the factory gate.

qa.q: What did Zeenat suggest posting?
qa.a: Zeenat suggested posting the home address of the factory manager.

qa.q: What did Ganga feel when everyone cheered?
qa.a: Ganga felt sick and uneasy, worried for the manager's children, but afraid to spoil things.

qa.q: Why was speaking up the next morning an act of loyalty?
qa.a: Ganga raised it early and kindly, before anything was posted, to protect people and the group's cause.

qa.q: How does Zeenat respond to Ganga's concern?
qa.a: Zeenat listens, thinks, and invites Ganga to raise it at the meeting, suspecting others feel the same.

grounding: A first-person account of hesitating to question a close-knit group's harmful plan, then dissenting early and kindly so the movement chose a safer path.

passage: Note from Noor, faculty adviser to the students' housing rights group, Friday. Today's planning meeting could have gone badly. The group, angry after the eviction notices, proposed telling residents that the municipal survey was a 'trick to demolish their homes', to get more people to the rally. It wasn't true; the survey was routine. I watched Hemant, one of the most committed volunteers, go quiet and stare at his notebook. He clearly disagreed and was afraid of seeming disloyal; the group has become like family to him. I didn't speak for him. After a few minutes he said, voice shaking, 'We can't lie to the people we're fighting for. If they find out, they'll stop trusting us.' There was a silence. Then two others agreed. The group rewrote the flyer with the true facts about the notices. Afterwards I told Hemant that disagreeing early is loyalty too. He looked relieved. I'll keep an eye on how the group handles dissent.

qa.q: What did the group propose telling residents?
qa.a: They proposed saying the municipal survey was a 'trick to demolish their homes'.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as he stared at his notebook?
qa.a: Hemant felt torn and afraid of seeming disloyal, though he disagreed.

qa.q: What made Hemant's dissent effective?
qa.a: He spoke early and calmly named the ethical and practical problem, others joined, and the flyer was rewritten truthfully.

qa.q: What would change for the residents if the false flyer went out?
qa.a: They might come to the rally on a lie and later stop trusting the group.

grounding: An adviser's note shows a committed volunteer overcoming fear of seeming disloyal to object early to a dishonest tactic, and the group changing course.
